plain_definition: A model has learned the particular examples it was trained on rather than the pattern behind them. It does well on data it has seen and badly on data it has not.
technical_explanation: A model has enough capacity to represent noise in the training set as though it were signal. Training error keeps falling while error on held-out data starts rising — the gap between the two is the symptom. It is driven by model capacity relative to the amount and diversity of training data, not by any single setting, which is why the fixes range from collecting more data through simplifying the model to constraining it with regularisation or stopping training earlier.
example: A classifier that reaches 99% on its training reviews and 71% on reviews it has never seen has memorised phrasing peculiar to the training set. The 28-point gap is the finding, not the 99%.
common_misconception: That a high training score is evidence of a good model. It is evidence of nothing at all on its own: a model that stored every training example verbatim would score perfectly and be useless.

plain_definition: Deliberately constraining a model so it cannot fit its training data too closely. You accept slightly worse performance on data you have in exchange for better performance on data you do not.
technical_explanation: Any technique that adds a preference for simpler solutions. Most commonly a penalty on parameter magnitude is added to the loss: L2 shrinks weights toward zero and spreads influence across features; L1 drives some weights exactly to zero and so performs feature selection. Dropout, early stopping, data augmentation and smaller architectures are all regularisation in the same sense — they reduce effective capacity even though none adds a penalty term.
example: Increasing the L2 penalty on a linear model usually raises training error and lowers held-out error, up to a point. Past that point both rise, and you have constrained the model past the pattern it was supposed to learn.
common_misconception: That more regularisation is safer. Too much causes underfitting, which is just as wrong and harder to spot, because both training and validation scores look consistently mediocre rather than suspiciously divergent.

plain_definition: Precision asks: of the things the model flagged, how many were right? Recall asks: of the things it should have flagged, how many did it find? Improving one usually costs the other.
technical_explanation: Both are computed from the counts of true positives, false positives and false negatives. Precision is TP / (TP + FP) — the reliability of a positive prediction. Recall is TP / (TP + FN) — the coverage of the actual positives. They trade off against each other through the decision threshold: lowering it flags more things, raising recall and lowering precision. Which matters more is a property of the problem, not of the model.
example: A spam filter with high precision and low recall rarely mislabels a real email but lets spam through. Reversed, it catches nearly all the spam and occasionally bins something important. Which failure you prefer is a product decision, not a modelling one.
common_misconception: That accuracy summarises both. On imbalanced data it summarises neither: if one class is 99% of the data, predicting it always gives 99% accuracy with zero recall on the class you actually cared about.

plain_definition: A single number combining precision and recall, so two models can be ranked without choosing between them first. It is deliberately harsh on models that are good at one and bad at the other.
technical_explanation: The harmonic mean of precision and recall. The harmonic mean is used rather than the arithmetic mean because it is dominated by the smaller of the two values: a model with precision 1.0 and recall 0.0 has an arithmetic mean of 0.5 but an F1 of 0. For multi-class problems the averaging strategy matters enormously — macro-F1 weights every class equally, micro-F1 weights every example equally, and the two can tell opposite stories on imbalanced data.
example: Precision 0.9 with recall 0.1 gives F1 of about 0.18, not 0.5. That is the point: the model is not half good.
common_misconception: That a single F1 figure describes a multi-class model. Without saying whether it is macro or micro averaged, the number is not comparable to anyone else's.

plain_definition: Splitting your data several different ways and training a model on each split, so your estimate of how good it is does not depend on one lucky division.
technical_explanation: In k-fold cross-validation the data is partitioned into k parts; the model is trained k times, each time holding out a different part for evaluation. The reported score is the mean, and the spread across folds is at least as informative — a large spread means your estimate is unstable and any comparison against another model is on thin ground. Structured data needs structured splitting: grouped splits when records share a source, and forward-chaining splits when data is ordered in time.
example: Five-fold cross-validation giving 0.81 with a spread of ±0.01 is a very different claim from 0.81 with a spread of ±0.12, even though both report the same mean.

code_example.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

# Pass the whole pipeline, not a pre-fitted model:
# any preprocessing must be refitted inside every fold.
scores = cross_val_score(pipeline, X, y, cv=5)
print(scores.mean(), scores.std())

common_misconception: That cross-validation removes the need for a final held-out test set. It does not: once you have used the folds to choose a model, those folds have informed your decision, and only data untouched by that process gives an honest final estimate.

plain_definition: Information that would not be available at prediction time has found its way into training. The model looks excellent and will fail the moment it is used for real.
technical_explanation: Leakage takes two broad forms. Preprocessing leakage happens when a transformation is fitted on all the data before splitting, so statistics from the test set influence the training set — scaling and vectorising are the usual culprits. Target leakage happens when a feature encodes the answer, often through something recorded only after the outcome was known. Both produce validation scores that are unreachable in deployment, and both are invisible unless you go looking.
example: Fitting a TF-IDF vectoriser on the full corpus and then splitting means the vocabulary was chosen using test documents. The score rises, and nothing about the model got better.

code_example.code:
# Leaks: the vectoriser saw every document before the split.
X = vectoriser.fit_transform(all_documents)
X_train, X_test = train_test_split(X)

# Correct: split first, and let the pipeline refit per fold.
train, test = train_test_split(all_documents)
pipeline.fit(train)

common_misconception: That a suspiciously good result is good news. An unexpected jump in score is far more often leakage than insight, and it is worth assuming so until you have ruled it out.

plain_definition: Cutting text into the small units a model actually reads. Those units are usually not words — they are word fragments chosen by an algorithm.
technical_explanation: A tokeniser maps a string to a sequence of integer ids drawn from a fixed vocabulary. Modern systems use subword schemes such as byte-pair encoding, WordPiece or Unigram, which build the vocabulary from frequent character sequences. This is a deliberate trade-off: a larger vocabulary means shorter sequences but a bigger embedding table, and a smaller one means the reverse. Because the vocabulary is fixed at training time, unseen words are split into fragments rather than lost, which is why models handle novel words at all.
example: A made-up word like "flurbulent" is split into several fragments the model has seen before. That is why it can process it, and why it may handle it oddly.
common_misconception: That tokens are words. They are not, and the difference explains a great deal of otherwise baffling behaviour — why character-level tasks are hard, why token counts do not match word counts, and why costs are quoted per token.

plain_definition: A list of numbers representing a piece of text, image or item, arranged so that things with similar meaning end up close together.
technical_explanation: A learned map from discrete objects to points in a continuous vector space, where geometric proximity approximates semantic relatedness. Embeddings are learned as a by-product of some training objective — predicting neighbouring words, matching captions to images, distinguishing related from unrelated pairs — and what "similar" means is determined entirely by that objective. Similarity is usually measured by cosine of the angle between vectors rather than by distance, which makes it insensitive to magnitude.
example: Embed twenty documents and query for a topic that appears in none of them by name. If the nearest result is still the right document, that is the property keyword search lacks.
common_misconception: That an embedding captures meaning in general. It captures whatever its training objective rewarded — an embedding trained to match products to searches encodes something quite different from one trained on encyclopaedia text, and neither is neutral.

plain_definition: A way for a model to decide which parts of its input matter most for each part of its output, instead of compressing everything into one fixed summary.
technical_explanation: Each position produces a query, a key and a value. Compatibility between a query and every key gives a set of weights, and the output at that position is the weighted sum of the values. Because every position can attend to every other, path length between any two positions is constant rather than growing with distance, which is what makes long-range dependencies learnable. Multiple attention heads run in parallel so different heads can specialise on different relationships.
example: Resolving what "it" refers to in a sentence requires looking back at a specific earlier noun. Attention lets the model weight that noun heavily for that position and largely ignore the rest.
common_misconception: That attention weights are an explanation of the model's reasoning. They show where information was drawn from, which is not the same as why an output was produced, and the research on treating them as explanations is not settled.

plain_definition: The neural network design that most current language and vision models are built from. Its defining feature is that it uses attention instead of processing a sequence step by step.
technical_explanation: A stack of identical blocks, each combining multi-head self-attention with a position-wise feed-forward network, wrapped in residual connections and normalisation. Because it has no inherent notion of order, position must be injected explicitly. Three families exist: encoder-only models that read bidirectionally and suit classification, decoder-only models that predict the next token and suit generation, and encoder-decoder models for transduction. Removing recurrence is what makes training parallelisable across a sequence, which is arguably why the architecture won.
example: The same block structure, stacked more times with wider layers, spans models from a few million parameters to hundreds of billions. That uniformity is much of its practical appeal.
common_misconception: That transformer means large language model. The architecture is used for vision, audio, protein structure and time series, and plenty of transformers are small enough to train on a laptop.

plain_definition: Taking a model someone else trained and continuing to train it on your own data, so it specialises without starting from nothing.
technical_explanation: Training resumes from pretrained weights, usually with a much smaller learning rate and far less data than the original run. Full fine-tuning updates every parameter and produces a complete model copy per task, which becomes impractical at scale. Parameter-efficient methods instead freeze the base weights and train a small number of added parameters, keeping one shared base model. Fine-tuning changes behaviour and format reliably; it is a poor and expensive way to add facts.
example: A general model fine-tuned on a few thousand labelled support tickets learns your categories and tone. It does not thereby learn your product documentation.
common_misconception: That fine-tuning is how you give a model new knowledge. For facts, retrieval is usually cheaper, more accurate and far easier to update — fine-tuning is for changing how a model behaves, not what it knows.

plain_definition: Running a trained model to get an answer, as opposed to training it. It is what happens every time someone actually uses the system.
technical_explanation: The forward pass alone, with no gradient computation and no weight updates. Its engineering profile is the opposite of training's: training is a batch job you run occasionally and can restart, while inference is latency-sensitive, runs continuously, and dominates lifetime cost for any deployed system. For generative models it is inherently sequential — each token depends on the previous one — which is why techniques like caching intermediate state matter so much in practice.
example: A model that trains once for a week may then serve requests for years. Almost all of the compute it ever consumes is inference.
common_misconception: That inference is the easy part because the hard maths is done. Cost, latency and reliability at inference time are where most production systems actually struggle.

plain_definition: When a language model states something fluent, confident and false. It is not lying — it has no notion of truth to depart from.
technical_explanation: A consequence of the training objective. A model trained to produce probable continuations will produce a probable-looking citation, statistic or API call whether or not one exists, because plausibility and accuracy are different properties and only the first is optimised. Grounding output in retrieved sources reduces the rate substantially but does not eliminate it: a model can still misread, over-generalise from, or contradict a passage it was given.
example: Asked for a reference, a model may produce a citation with a real-sounding author, a plausible title and a well-formed identifier that resolves to nothing. Every surface feature is right except the existence of the paper.
common_misconception: That better prompting or a larger model eliminates it. Both reduce the rate; neither removes the cause, which is that the objective never rewarded being right. Any workflow that cannot survive a confident false answer needs verification outside the model.

plain_definition: Looking up relevant documents first, then asking a model to answer using them. The point is that the answer can be traced back to a source.
technical_explanation: A retrieval step selects passages relevant to a query, and those passages are placed in the model's context along with the question. This separates what the model knows from what it can look up, which makes knowledge updatable without retraining and makes provenance possible. Quality is dominated by retrieval: if the right passage is never retrieved, no amount of prompting recovers the answer, so evaluating retrieval separately is the single most useful thing to do.
example: Ask a question the documents cannot answer. A well-built system says it does not know; a poorly built one answers anyway from the model's parameters, and nothing in the output distinguishes the two cases.
common_misconception: That grounding makes output trustworthy. It shifts the failure mode: the model can still misread a passage, and a citation can point at text that does not support the claim attached to it.

plain_definition: The data a deployed model sees stops resembling the data it was trained on. The model has not changed; the world has.
technical_explanation: Several distinct things get the same name. Covariate shift is a change in the input distribution with the input-to-output relationship intact. Label shift is a change in the frequency of outcomes. Concept drift is a change in the relationship itself, and is the hardest because the model is now wrong rather than merely uncalibrated. Detecting shift needs monitoring of input statistics and, where labels eventually arrive, of realised outcomes — uptime metrics reveal none of it.
example: A model trained on newswire performs far worse on social media text. Nothing broke; the input distribution simply moved somewhere the training data never described.
common_misconception: That a model degrades gradually and visibly. It can fail sharply the day an upstream system changes format, and nothing in the serving metrics will say so.

plain_definition: A deployed model getting worse over time even though nobody changed it. Its assumptions have quietly stopped holding.
technical_explanation: The observable consequence of distribution shift: measured performance declines while the artefact is unchanged. Detecting it requires ground truth, which usually arrives late or not at all, so monitoring generally combines lagging outcome metrics with leading proxies such as input statistics, prediction distributions and confidence. Feedback loops make this worse — when a model's own outputs influence the data it later sees, drift can be self-inflicted rather than externally caused.
example: A recommendation model shapes what users see, which shapes what they click, which becomes its next training data. The distribution it trains on is now partly its own output.
common_misconception: That retraining on recent data always fixes it. If a feedback loop is the cause, retraining on data the model itself shaped can entrench the problem instead.

plain_definition: Whether a model's stated confidence matches how often it is actually right. A well-calibrated model that says 70% is correct about 70% of the time.
technical_explanation: A property distinct from accuracy: a model can rank cases correctly while its probabilities are systematically wrong, and a model can be well calibrated while being mediocre. It is assessed by bucketing predictions by confidence and comparing each bucket's stated probability against its observed accuracy, usually visualised as a reliability diagram. Modern neural networks tend to be overconfident, and post-hoc methods such as temperature scaling can correct much of this without retraining.
example: Take every prediction the model made with about 80% confidence. If far fewer than 80% turned out correct, the number cannot be used for thresholding or triage.
common_misconception: That a softmax output is a probability. It sums to one, which is not the same thing, and treating an uncalibrated score as a probability quietly breaks any decision rule built on a threshold.

plain_definition: A measure of how surprised a language model is by text. Lower means the text looked more predictable to the model.
technical_explanation: The exponential of the average negative log-likelihood the model assigns per token. It can be read loosely as the effective number of equally likely choices the model was weighing at each step. Because it is computed per token, it depends entirely on the tokeniser: two models with different vocabularies produce perplexities that cannot be compared, and neither can perplexities measured on different corpora.
example: A model reporting perplexity 20 on one corpus and 45 on another has not necessarily got worse. The second corpus may simply be less predictable text.
common_misconception: That lower perplexity means a more useful model. It measures fit to a text distribution, not helpfulness, correctness or safety, and it can improve while the things you care about get worse.

plain_definition: A family of scores for summarisation that measure how much wording a generated summary shares with a reference one. It rewards overlap, not quality.
technical_explanation: ROUGE-N measures n-gram overlap between candidate and reference; ROUGE-L uses the longest common subsequence, so it is somewhat order-aware. Being overlap-based, it cannot recognise a correct summary phrased differently from the reference, and it cannot detect a fluent summary that is factually wrong. Agreement with human judgement is weak enough that a ROUGE improvement should not be reported as a quality improvement without human evaluation alongside it.
example: On news summarisation, simply copying the first few sentences of the article scores surprisingly well. Any system that fails to beat that baseline convincingly has demonstrated very little.
common_misconception: That a higher ROUGE score means a better summary. It means more word overlap with one particular reference, which was itself often written as a teaser rather than as a faithful summary.
